author: @randm4246
text: Excellent job breakdown. The one plot contrivance that I haven't heard anyone look into or mention is the wormhole paradox: In the film, humans could not have survived the destruction of Earth without the wormhole, but how did humans evolve past the great filter to get to the point that they were able to construct the wormhole without the wormhole? We can mess with the relativity of space time all we want, but without the wormhole we wouldn't have survived and evolved to create the wormhole. It's a catch 22. I understand that you hypothesize that it was AI that was able to place the wormhole for us, but we wouldn't have gotten to the point where we could have fallen into the black hole to bridge that gap without the wormhole being there in the first place. What I think happened is that a race of humans from either another planet that has existed for far longer than we have had found Earth and decided to help us, or more likely it was another race of humans from a parallel universe's Earth that placed the wormhole to assist humanity in our universe.

text: I think what needs to be clarified is that time dilation refers to only the perception or realization of time being slower. Time itself is not what is able to decelerate. This is all about gravity’s affect on matter. “Dilation” is just the phenomenon of light itself being slowed down. Redshifts are certainly fascinating and hard enough to comprehend. The only way you can stand behind dilation is by saying we can time travel. That can’t reasonably be argued beyond a theoretical level. Remember, time is not what’s malleable: only our perception of it is. Also, don’t misinterpret what it means for clocks to tick slower or faster. Atomic clocks rely on a specific measure of gravity to give us the common “second”. At varying gravities, the frequency of the atomic radiation and be faster or slower. I’m as fascinated by the time dilation enigma just as much as anybody else, but we can’t romanticize it to a point where we accept nonsensical concepts that are not proven. Also, the GPS clock argument is the most shallow argument. They simply tick slower. The satellites themselves do not experience time slower.

author: @angelamartzen7499
text: I can see how some people didn't like the "love" aspect of this movie because on the surface it sounds corny and contrived. But if you set aside the urge to roll your eyes at any and every utterance of the word love, you would see that Brand's speech makes sense. If Cooper did not have a family that he cared about, a daughter that he so desperately wanted to get back to, then he would not have tried as hard as he could to complete their mission. Doing something for the good of all humanity is honestly too big for most people. He never even wanted to go on this mission in the first place. You can tell that by the time they get to Gargantua, Cooper is really only thinking about his daughter... if he ends up saving the rest of humanity then that's a bonus, but his real goal was to get back to his daughter. It's not selfish, it's human. We have the instinct to protect ourselves and our young. It's unrealistic to think that in a time of desperation and survival, that we would be taking every single other person into account. We prioritize what's most important to us. If your child was trapped in a burning building with several other random people, who would you save first? Your own child of course. If you could then help save others then maybe you would, but your goal is to save yourself and your loved ones first. Even heroes are not textbook perfect individuals. Brand was determined to get to Edmunds planet because she loved him and yes she made some poor decisions based on this feeling, but that just shows how love itself is a driving force to motivate someone to do something, good or bad. If you listen to Brand speaking about love, she openly points out how love can be nonsensical when you try to break it down logically, "We love people who have died. Where's the social utility in that?" and "I'm drawn across the universe to someone I haven't seen in a decade, who I know is probably dead." She is just acknowledging the undeniable fact that love compels us and it's bigger than what we believe it to be.

text: Interstellar (2014) Ending Explained: Part - 2 Interstellar me Cooper Gargantua Black Hole ke andar girta hai aur singularity ke paas pahunchta hai. Kaise Pahucha? 1. Tesseract Scene: Jab Cooper aur TARS Gargantua ke accretion disk me enter karte hain, tab extreme gravity aur time dilation ke wajah se wo singularity ki taraf accelerate hote hain. Normally, Black Hole me girne wale kisi bhi object ka spaghettification ho jata hai (matlab, wo infinite stretch ho jata hai). Par movie me Cooper spaghettification se bach jata hai kyunki usse fifth-dimensional beings (bulk beings) bacha lete hain. 2. Fifth-Dimensional Tesseract: Ye beings higher-dimensional entities hain jo time ko ek physical dimension ki tarah dekh sakte hain. Unhone Cooper ke liye ek Tesseract structure banaya, jisme uska consciousness 5D spacetime me freely move kar sakta hai. Wahan Cooper apni beti Murph se contact karta hai through gravitational signals (watch ke second hand ke motion se). Kya Ye Scientifically Possible Hai? Agar Cooper directly singularity me girta, to Quantum Mechanics ke rules ke mutabik uska existence collapse ho jata. Kip Thorne (physicist, jo movie ke scientific advisor the) ne kaha ki Singularity tak koi bhi survive nahi kar sakta. Par movie me extra-dimensional intervention dikhaya gaya hai, jo theoretically higher dimensions aur brane-world physics me possible ho sakta hai. Matlab, Cooper singularity tak physically nahi pahucha, balki higher-dimensional beings ne usse ek safe 5D space (Tesseract) me place kar diya, jisse usne past me interact kiya aur Murph ko Gravity Equation ka hint diya.

text: This is of only 3 films I give a 10/10. I am VERY harsh when reviewing and critiquing movies but this one was a 10/10 for me. The only other films I give a 10/10 are (and in order) Interstellar, The Dark Knight, and 2001 A Space Odyssey. Yes, I am a bit partial to space movies but something like Gravity I would give a 5/10 at most. Nolan is my favorite director of all time (with Kubrick at second and maybe Speilberg or Tarantino at 3rd/4th). Interstellar hits every single criterion perfectly. I thought Matthew McConaughey and Anne Hathaway's performances were a 10/10. Obviously, the visuals were a 10/10, the plot was a 10/10, and who could forget possibly the greatest 10/10 score of all time. I mean there isn't a single lacking point in this entire movie. Nolan is a fucking genius and what's so special about this movie particularly, was that it wasn't just another space movie. This movie LITERALLY revolutionized how we think about space, Nolan brought on the greatest living Astro Physiscts for this movie and REVOLUTIONIZED how we think about space, black holes, and gravity. If you haven't read up on the real-life implications of this movie, I highly recommend it. This movie actually changed what we think about relativity and the black hole scene in particular actually revised our understanding of black holes. Like how can you argue this movie isn't anything other than perfection? It was not only a 10/10 film-wise, but literally changed how we looked at space, relatively, gravity, and black holes. What other film did that?

text: This is the best analysis of Interstellar there is. It mirrors my thoughts that I've had on the film perfectly, thoughts that I've had to argue with people about constantly. There are so many people, including film critics, who claim to be smart and look down on Interstellar who deride the film as rubbish. Their criticism often includes making fun of the film for supposedly claiming that "love is the fifth dimension" which shows a complete lack of understanding of what the film was trying to say. Time and time again I have said to people that the film isn't saying that love is the fifth dimension or anything like that, it's saying that the bulk beings have no way of communicating their important message because they have access to infinite time and they need the connection between Cooper and his daughter to communicate that message in order to save the human race. THAT is why love is important in the film. It's nice to see that at least one other person ACTUALLY understands what's happening in the film. Great video.

author: @burstofsanity
text: I still feel that this film is middling at best. The entire premise is non-sensical. It's the same old, the Earth is dying so let's go somewhere else. Every planet they visit is orders of magnitude worse than Mars for habitability and even if they found the perfect planet to rebuild humanity on the "space station" solution was never an option even though the movie says otherwise. If you can't keep the blight from infecting everything on Earth, how are you going to ensure the space station is free of it? Logically, the whole movie is a non-sensical mess not just the ending. The Wheeler's delayed choice experiment segment sounds like a "quantum frequency of water" level of misunderstanding of what the experiment actually shows. **Time travel is not possible** and claiming this experiment in anyway gives hope that one day it may be possible, or that it could somehow justify the magic black hole in the movie is disappointing. This movie has just about the same amount of science in it as Signs and just about as much magic, just slightly less biblical. Just accept that the movie is fiction with the aesthetics of science. I would be far less interested in people's take on this movie if it was treated more like Star Wars than like Cosmos.

text: I think it is possible that two planets have a difference of gravity as strong, therefore of time dilation as in the movie but not in this way. The difference in time dilation does not only depend on the mass and therefore on the gravitational force of the planet in question but on everything else! If two planets have exactly the same mass, but one is next to a black hole in the center of a galaxy, and the second planet is at the border of the galaxy, so much further away than the black hole, then there will be a real time dilation even if these two planets have the same mass. Because the first planet will be affected by the gravitational force of the black hole. So if two planets have more or less the same mass and therefore the same gravitational force, but if one is next to a black hole and the other one is not, then I think that it is possible that there is a real time dilation to the point that one hour on the world close to the black hole represents 7 years in the world that has no black hole next to it I believe that this is what happened in the movie because there was the black hole Gargantua next to this watery planet. But I don't claim to be right. It's just that I find it logical that for time dilation, the fact that one planet is next to a black hole and the other one is not has an impact even if both planets have the same mass.

This however, is not the case for Edmund's planet, it continues to run on its own time. Eventually, humans evolve into 5D beings on Edmund's planet and create the tesseract, once the tesseract was created, again, time is infinite and inconsequential as explained previously, allowing these 5D humans to manipulate time to their favour and interact with Cooper in different timelines (past and future, that's why there were 2 Coopers). Why did they choose Cooper to be the key person to enter the tesseract? Because Brand was the kickstarter of the human species on Edmund's planet and she must have relayed the information about Cooper's existence to the humans there before they evolved. Cooper then entered the tesseract, manipulated time to contact Murphy and pass the quantum data to her allowing her to solve the gravity equation, eventually saving the humans on Earth. Thus, to conclude, Cooper, by making the decision to go into the black hole and abandoning Brand to Edmund's planet, allowed the human species to restart and evolve on Edmund's planet, then the humans on Edmund's planet, made the decision to save Earth by manipulating time

author: @kaisokusekkendou1498
text: The ending "solution" inside the black hole makes sense to me in a certain way... I'd once watched a video on the physics of a black hole, explaining how it's essentially a flip on how our own reality works. We exist in a spatial dimension that is locked on a single course through time. However, once in a black hole, you are instead locked on a single course in spatial dimensions... and the math indicates that shifting your perspective, you'd be able to observe all time in the same way we travel freely in space. Note "observe", not interact. Where "love" comes into this is based on the two presumptions the movie makes (where we need to suspend our disbelief): 1. That Cooper and TARS could survive entering a black hole. 2. That something in the human consciousness was able to exert influence over this new form of dimensional experience. If we accept those things, then "love" will drive his sub-conscious to bring him to his daughter, to his one regret.. the moment he left her in that room. So in an infinite reality of time and space, his unique emotional background drove him to precisely where he could do something.. and trigger the final concession: that gravity can be influenced beyond space-time limits like a black hole. Since this is the concession that is basically the macguffin that resolves the main plot too, it's fine I think. Honestly, his going into the black hole and influencing time and space can mean this is a closed time loop scenario. There doesn't even have to be "special future humans" or "aliens"... it was literally Cooper going into the black hole, and his emotional subconscious, that spat out the wormhole and started this whole thing in the first place. His "hand passing through their ship going through the wormhole" at the beginning indicates his influence is in there somewhere. I feel it's a perfect resolution to a story of humanity that deals with hope, fighting in spite of despair, and an "I'll do it myself" gumption of a pioneering man of the land.

author: @quietfolk3920
text: As a movie enthusiast and a huge Nolan fan, I was a little disappointed, but very inspired. I think Nolan succeeded in what he wanted. When I stepped out of the theater, A LOT of people were screaming in amazement. Everyone was just so...touched by it, so awed, and I think that was what really makes the movie. For that reason, I think it should be getting higher praise, maybe not as a movie, but definitely for what its trying to do. However, I don't think many critics and serious movie enthusiasts will get it, because I feel like it was never meant to be the perfect movie we expected, its meant to be a spark to something beyond a movie. We were expecting a cinematic masterpiece, when it was reaching for something else. Don't just think about the movie you saw, think "the future of the human race." That, or Nolan was just not in his game :P I would also like to say that just because you couldn't understand the science in the dialogue, it doesn't make the movie bad. One of the main goals of the movie was to present a scenario with as much accuracy as possible, making its message about humans even more inspiring because its telling us that the amazing things we saw in the movie are very possible.

author: @aairahplays
text: What if Interstellar's "They" aren’t just future humans, but actually the evolved descendants (embryo's) of Brand’s colony on Edmunds’ planet? Think about it: Future humans helped Cooper so Murph could solve the gravity equation, leading to Cooper Station. But why? Because Cooper Station ensures that Cooper reaches Brand. And if Brand’s colony fails, They would never exist. Murph sending Cooper to Brand wasn’t just about love or closure—she knew Brand’s colony had to succeed. Surviving alone on a barren planet with only embryos would be incredibly difficult, and Cooper could be the key to making it work. By going to Brand, Cooper unknowingly ensured the future of humanity. So, They interfered to make sure events unfolded correctly. The entire cycle was about self-preservation. They ensured Earth’s people were saved, not just for survival, but so Cooper would eventually reach Brand and help establish the very civilization that would later intervene. This also means Plan B wasn’t a backup—it was always the real future. The loop is self-sustaining: Future humans exist because they made sure their own ancestors survived.

author: @stupor_mundi
text: Good video, good points! I thought it very thought-provoking how Nolan introduced love as a kind of powerful force with unique properties that trancends time and space. I recall other two movies that essentially brought forward the exact same idea in different ways: one is of course Contact, the other is The Village. Contact is somewhat comparable to Interstellar in more obvious ways than The Village, so there's no point going into it, but The Village [warning: spoilers from this point] ends with the ultimate conclusion that love is a powerful guiding and supporting force that should be trusted. We explicitly see that in the scene when Ivy's father justifies letting her leave the village to get life-saving medicine for Lucius, whom she loves, when he says "She's more capable than most of us... And she is led by love. The world moves for love, it kneels before it in awe." He's basically saying that despite her disability they should trust that love - as a powerful driving force and source of strength - would open the path for her success. And it did, against all odds. I know The Village gets a lot of flak, perhaps in the same way Contact does (or even Interstellar, to some extent) for introducing love into the equation, but to deny the power of love would be like cutting off an essential part of our humanity, the human experience, maybe even the meaning of life. I think Brand in Interstellar is onto something.

author: @Mystikan
text: The idea I got from the scenes inside the black hole is this: when you pass the event horizon, all paths lead to the singularity. At no point is it possible to get further away from the singularity, or even to remain at a constant distance from it. This means that the dimension of space in the direction of the singularity becomes timelike, so time as experienced outside the black hole must become spacelike. This means that he can move back and forth through time in the same manner he normally could through a given dimension of space - at least for as long as he has before he becomes spaghettified by proximity to the singularity, which is his inescapable future. So the "library" inside the black hole to me represented universal time as a spacelike dimension in which he could move at will, because his formerly spacelike path to the singularity had become his axis of time. This is what enabled him to travel back in time to his daughter's childhood and leave the message "STAY" on her bookshelf before he was crushed by the singularity.

author: @pjboyle8369
text: Amazing movie, one of my favourites. An aspect I really enjoy is the connection between the fight scene of Mann vs Cooper and the "first handshake". Mann says to Cooper, after the breaking of the helmet and subsequent slow suffocation, "Do you see your children?" - a common held belief that you see those you love as you are about to die; deathbed visions. Cooper, at that moment, is not having any vision because we know he is not dying. Later in the film, during the tesseract scene, when the message is sent to Murphy via the watch, the tesseract then closes. Cooper asks TARS, when the approaching collapse is upon him, "What happens now?" and a bright light surrounds him and gives the impression that his life is over. Of course, he then travels back through the wormhole, passing the Endurance on the way back, and reaches out, and takes Brand's hand. I often wonder why Cooper saw Brand, in his apparent "dying moments", and not another. With the recurring theme of love, I like to think that this is a reference to his love for Brand; an element confirmed in the Murphy and Cooper reunion where she says "You can go" and prompts him to seek Brand.

text: Two things I'd like to add; a fun observation and a theory: 1) The watch that Murph had was a Hamilton Field Khaki MECHANICAL watch. That's important, because if it was a digital watch, as you might expect in the future, there would have been no way for Cooper to relay the data for Murph to find. 2) So, Plan A, and presumably Plan B were both successful. My fun theory is that it WASN'T Murph's Plan A that lead to 4th Dimensional future humanity. Instead it was Plan B with Cooper, Brand, and their embryos. This is an interesting thought because A) it COULD mean that humanity effectively split into two different evolutionary paths, perhaps unbeknownst of each other. If these two humanities developed for 1000, or 10,000 of years separately and eventually found each other again, how different would they be? And B) because it could have meant Murph WASN'T who the future beings were counting on to save them. It was actually Cooper & Brand, contrary to Coopers "revelation" in the tesseract.

author: @michaelzoran
text: QUESTION: On Mann's planet, after Brand has rescued Cooper, we see Mann's base explodes. This apparently kills Dr. Romily and CASE. I have read online this happens because CASE was programmed with the truth about Dr. Mann's planet not being inhabitable, and that the security clearance that was needed from a person had a form of boobytrap that automatically triggered an explosion - which killed Dr. Romily (the person) and CASE (the robot that was boobytrapped by Dr. Mann). If that information is true, it is VERY COMPLEX and NONE OF IT was explained in the movie! ... Why was none of that explained in the movie? How were we supposed to know all of that simply from seeing Dr. Mann attack Cooper? My personal interpretation was nothing like that at all when I saw Dr. Mann attack Cooper. My personal interpretation was that Cooper learned Professor Brand had been lying to him about Plan A. As a result, Cooper planned to return to Earth with the ship in order to see his kids again. My personal interpretation was that Dr. Mann was being unselfish and was not willing to allow Cooper to place his personal selfish desire to see his kids ahead of what was best for the entire human species. My personal interpretation was that Dr. Mann had no choice but to make it seem like Cooper died in an accident, in order to save the entire human species with Plan B on Mann's planet - which Mann said was a healthy planet. My personal interpretation was that Dr. Mann was left with no choice but to attack Cooper, because Cooper's ship was needed on Dr. Mann's planet in order to help Plan B succeed. I cannot find any spot in the movie where it "says" or even "implies" that Dr. Mann "boobytrapped" the CASE robot. The movie does say Dr. Mann "was lying," but that could be about anything. It makes no mention of CASE being boobytrapped. And the movie even talks about how the CASE robot was destroyed, but didn't seem to care that Dr. Romily died, too. All of that was VERY CONFUSING, because it needed a LOT MORE EXPLANATION. ... Considering the movie is 2 Hours 49 Minutes long, the writers definitely SHOULD HAVE included that information. If there are scenes I did not interpret correctly or pieces of information I missed, please share them with me so I understand it better.

text: There are two things in the film that didn't gell for me. Firstly, it sets the beginning as a battle against the blight. Now I know that this was just a pretext to getting the characters into space, however it created a promise about what dilemma would be overcome, and failed to properly address it. Furthermore, what was resolved was the finding of a solution for quantum gravity, but we don't really understand how this solves what is essentially a resource problem. Linked to the resource problem, the whole distopian authoritarianism complete with information control felt like another unresolved problem promise (or perhaps something resolved off screen). These two problems were promptly forgotten about, in favour of a space adventure, with some newly manufactured problems to overcome, like Mann and the two failed planets. Had it started in the new system, these crises wouldn't have felt so manufactured. Secondly, apart from "love", why did Cooper need to go back? To put it another way, why did plan B need to continue? Humanity was already thriving in space back at Sol.

The vast majority of scientists are afraid to say "I do not know" because of peers. author: @chrisalex001
text: I'm sorry, but Interstellar was not a good movie. Encounters of the third kind was, even Inception (as dark as it was). The great acting did not deliver believable characters. That can only happen when the writing is bad. First of all, why would humanity leave its own planet for who knows what's outthere (even despite the accurately depicted dust storms caused by the erosion of the soil and atmospheric destabilization caused by global warming)? The whole tessaract thing was cool and very interesting, but Michael Cain was just not believable as a great scientist, not like Jack Lemmon was as a nuclear physicist in The China Syndrome or Gregory Peck as the director of NASA in Marooned, or Lindsay Crouse as a climate scientist in The Arrival (1996), or Jodie foster in Contact, or Helen Hunt in Twister, or Armand Assante as Odysseus in the 90s Odyssey, or Richard Harris as Dumbledore in Harry Potter and Sulla in 2002 Julius Caesar, or Richard Burton in Where Eagles Dare, or Brad Pitt, Brian Cox, and Peter O'toole in their respective roles in the movie Troy from the 2000s, should I go on? Matthew McConaughey acted very well, yet his savior role just didn't feel believable, not really. The movie felt like an exercise in great acting even if the audience can't truly identify why the strong emotions being felt are actually felt even with Hans Zimmerman's music. It's as if the audience felt strong emotions but does not really know why. Remember the last scene of Artificial Intelligence (Steven Spielberg)? Yeah, that kind of emotion is what I'm talking about. Also, Matt Damon (one of my favorite actors) acted very well, and his role should have been interesting on paper, and yet it wasn't. Anne Hathaway, who was the best character in my opinion, still felt like she was in the wrong movie. The movie remains very watchable because of its scientific accuracy (at least as close as it gets) but not the story. The movie simply did not convey the genuine believable emotions of a good story, not because of bad acting, but because of bad writing (including what most people would consider an exaggerated nitpick: the fact that when Cooper came to see an old Murph, his own family did not recognize him or wanted to know who he was, or the fact that he didn't ask about them. That might seem normal in this culture but extremely dysfunctional and abnormal in most other countries (I know what you'rethinking but actually having Cooper show much more interest in his descendants before being alone with Murph would have given the scene a far richer touch of authenticity. Great directing and writing often involves including the obvious and predictable but in extraordinary ways because genius is nothing more than taking the ordinary subtlyinto the extraordinary.. I just came to say all this. BTW, if you want a movie that transcends time (The Fifth Element)

author: @roddaman7545
text: @4:15: A thought, and I'll risk sounding like a Luddite: Time is merely context, the inevitability that one thing happens after another that orders events from a galactic scale to an atomic one. It is monolithic, unchanging, inflexible, the ultimate objective continuum. It is our experience of time and the measurement of time and the pace of all thing taking place within time, that changed with gravity (4:23) or speed. If time itself slowed, you would not be able to return to the world in the time you left behind. The atomic clock that falls behind could never be reunited with it's faster sibling because it would always be 2 or 3 seconds ahead. Just as I cannot know what is happening in 2 seconds or 2 days, the clock from 2 seconds ahead would not exist in the reality of now. The concept conveyed in Interstellar toys with the idea of a sort of hub of time, where one can enter from one spoke and exit onto another, thereby jumping over those 2 seconds or 2 days mentioned above or the decades conveyed in the film (although they use a library, not a wheel). Cooper uses this hub to send a message from his time/space to his daughter's. However, in our routine observations (like the Atomic clocks) , we only experience a change in the rate of temporal processes, not a slowing of time itself. In the movie when Cooper returns to find his daughter an old woman, it is merely the differences in the processes of time that is experienced. He is there, in THAT time, in that moment so time itself did not slow for him or accelerate for her. If it had, he would be stuck in the time he left or she stuck in the time that would be.

text: Nice analysis of the conclusion of the film, mate! BTW: When I watched the film for the first time, I came to a quite simple conclusion: There doesn't necessarily have to be that much complexity, but it could also be just a very(!) well-told version of a classical Hero's journey: a bunch of people are going against all odds willingly because they're driven by a sense of determination to not roll just over and die, and they're lucky enough to succeed and are rewarded by living to see that their efforts were not in vain but did bear fruit as intended. Which means: the film could just be a nice story being told by narrators with the talents to do a good job (i.e. Nolan and his brother as well as the cast and crew). That doesn't mean I don't like different intepretations, on the contrary: I my opinion, one very important criterion which makes a film a good and rememberable one is: when a film motivates people who watched it to think and come to their own conclusions. Or as Christopher Nolan said it well: "it's there for you to make what you make of it". Which means interpretations like e.g. yours in the video isn't overanalyzing at all but just another point of view which made me think: "Hmmm... interesting, didn't think of that, but I like it". And that's the whole point: watching a film doesn't have to be something passive, but can (and should) stimulate people's imagination.

text: I believe that the point of the tesseract WAS a vessel that humans from far into the future built to save themselves from the past, maybe humans from previous missions that had become far more advanced than us or maybe something that we cannot comprehend, either way it was constructed to save humanity in my humble opinion and Cooper was the key to the lock. They had access to unlimited space and time but they could not manipulate access to the past because they did not have any ancestors with a “quantifiable connection” of love. Cooper’s love for his daughter did indeed transcend space, time, and anything else for that matter and that’s why they needed him to save humanity. Maybe the tesseract was a manipulation of light, storing pockets of time captured in beams of light going back trillions of years and spanning those beams of light far into the universe and beyond, the thing is we don’t know and we’ll never know. That’s the beauty of this film. It leaves so much to our imaginations because in the end, we cannot comprehend anything beyond earth. We only understand what we know and our laws of physics and matter and everything may not apply beyond our solar system, making anything possible and none of it understandable, even to the smartest of us. That’s what I love about Interstellar, it’s a masterpiece of the mind, something that makes you take a step back and reconsider what you really know and don’t know. And most important of all, it reminds us of just how small we are, how insignificant our existence is in the vast, open, and potentially unlimited sea of space. Maybe someday we’ll get there, venture far beyond the reaches of this universe to discover a new chapter in our existence, but for now, just dreaming of things like this movie depicts give me goosebumps and blows my imagination and reasoning into the air.

author: @BobSmith-dk8nw
text: I'm not a fan of ambiguous endings. I understand the idea. You get all vague so that the reader/viewer can make up their own ending - which like all those vague rock song lyrics makes them more popular. Personally, I think it's a cop out. The author couldn't come up with a good ending - so they get really vague and - OH MY! - they seem so profound!!!! I have more respect for and interest in - authors that can come up with a good ending. The problem with a lot of Sci-Fi is that it thinks it's got to come up with some Universe Shaking Conclusion ... when it doesn't. You don't have to save the Galaxy every time. You can just tell a story about people and the circumstances they are in - and that is good enough. But noooooo .... And so we come to all these vague bull shit endings where my reaction is - "I don't care." If all the author did was come up with some vague ending so he could seem profound ... I've seen that before. Now - up until Cooper goes in the Black Hole - this is a good movie. I thought that them having to make a choice and not being able to go to all the different spots was contrived. The mission should have been designed with enough resiliency that they could go around and pick everyone up or that they could make their findings and leave on their own. What was good - was the tidal wave scene where it's like "Oh! Shit!" - something unexpected (which would happen on exploratory vessels) pops up and can take them out. But - the worst - is the utter bull shit of "LOVE" conquering time and space ... I just fucking hate that. It isn't just that it's stupid. It's been done to death. Another thing I hate - is being tricked by the author. It's like ... so what ... you tricked the viewer. ANYONE can do that. You control all the information they have and how it's presented - tricking them into thinking one thing when you really intend another - is just a cheap, sleazy trick. I don't like being tricked. If all the last part of the movie was - was this guys death dream ... fuck it. I come to threads like this to see if the author has owned up to what he was doing. But if he hasn't then what's the point? We're never going to figure out it. All we can do is guess. If that is a form of entertainment where the author is intentionally creating something for us to worry our minds over ... well ... it's not a form of entertainment I enjoy. .

text: Definitely a subscriber. Despite the negative comments, I found that your video had a interesting idea for the outcome and interpretation of the movie. For me, I interpret the ending that these were not advanced humans millions of years into the future, that created the wormhole etc. I say this because if the population starting on Edmunds planet (with Brand starting the surrogacy) was so far evolved past our current species and created a wormhole and "tesseract," then it would create a paradox. I believe it's called the Bootstrap paradox? A good example of this paradox is if you were at home and received a book called "how to build a time machine" and built it over the course of 10 years or so..... You would wonder, "who could have sent me this book?" Then it dawns on you that, "hey, it was me! I could send myself and this book back in time, ten years to my younger self!" Paradox! You could only build the time machine if you discovered the book but you can only discover the book if you made the time machine.... it would be as if nobody has discovered the book or time machine and it would be stuck in this form of causal loop. Both of them cannot exist without the other. This is why I believe that instead of humans, it was a different form of advanced life. This still creates some issues with TARS attempting to relay the quantum data when he/she/it was inside the tesseract. It caused anomalies with Cooper's Ranger (causing a crash years ago in Earth-time), etc. Another plausible idea is having multiple or an infinite number of what we perceive as a universe. Example: you may have created a time machine with your own free will and sent the book back in time but instead you "traveled" into a different universe altogether, changing their version of time. Maybe time just doesn't exist? Maybe it's possible that everything that exists always had a past, present and future that was already set. Time is relative....we feel the present, remember the past and dream about the future.

text: Eric, you mentioned about The Bulk Beings being AI and because the director wanted to show us Black Holes and other phenomenal things beyond our comprehension, that they didn’t simply save earth in the beginning. My question is: Did evolved humans create those AI’s to help create the Tessaract? AND how did humans survive in the first place to get to the point of evolution so advanced that they could create an AI to help them make a worm hole and tessaract? AND are “They” in some dire situation that they would need to create these incredible things to save themselves also? Amelia Brand said: “To them the past could be a canyon they can climb into and the future a mountain they can climb up” meaning like climbing down a canyon, there are challenges, risks, and difficulties, but it is still possible. AND why would empathy be lacking if humans created that AI? Those are my thoughts and questions that whirl in my head as I watch this movie.

author: @idoittinkeringprojects9893
text: Dilation of time is real, though confusing. Dilation is detected in satellite systems over gps. However, detected is an anomaly over current belief, that time dilates proportionately at increasing speeds. The contention now is time does not only dilate but also expand. And heres my explaination. Time distortion is essentially due to the phenomenon of the doppler effect. That such is clearly observed over sound, the same rationale can be extended to light. In the doppler phenomenon, the pitch of the sound source is changed to higher or lower as it passes an observer . As like a fire engine, the sound of siren from afar progressively gets higher in pitch as it comes . After passing through, its siren sound gets lower in pitch as it goes . And, the firefighters on board do not hear any difference in siren sound. Such is because, sound waves within the fire engine remain unchanged Sound waves outside of the moving fire engine will distort. Coming Sound waves moving towards the observer compresss. Sound waves moving away expand . With a situation over light, imagine a rocket with a beam of light is approaching a space station , enroute to pass it. The doppler phenomenon will distort the beam of light towards higher frequency , then , after passing the space station , the beam will distort towards lower frequency . The astronaut in the space station will observe a blue shift on the beam of light when its coming towards. And a red shift when its going away. The astronaut in the rocket sees no difference. Then speed of light to all observation positions remain unchanged, while the distances between the rocket (light source) and space station (observer) changes from far to near then to far again. Such suggest time must have distorted to manifest the doppler phenomenon. c = d / t. That c is constant, it should mean when d is shortened, t will reduce proportionately. And certainly too, when d is lengthened, t will increase accordingly. This rationale confirms the distortion of time over movements of time frames relative to each other. However, the distortion is not only confined to dilation but should also include expansion. As the doppler effect exists in sound surroundings, it is suggested, time distortions do occur at such regular circumstances. The distortion of time is not too significant to cause much bother on earthy existence. Its significant over space and accountable when we need to compute consequences of space travel, time frames between planets, between star systems, galaxies etc.

text: The term 'Time Dilation' is a misnomer. It is an incorrect term and confuses the audience. Time is relative, but static. Using a term like Time Dilation, you are supposed to believe that time speeds up or slows down...which is absurd. Time is not a tangible item. It is not linear, and is not maleable or manipulated. Time cannot be increased or decreased. Instead, what is really happening is slowed animation, which is affecting matter... not time. General Relativity and Special Relativity easily explain this, but they refuse to explain it in movies. Do you time travel 8 hours every night when you sleep ? From your perspective, some days you lay down only to open your eyes for the next day's work.... and your mind does not feel that hours have passed. Same concept.. RELATIVITY. If the effects of time are slowed, are you slowing down time...NO. This is not a hard concept. Time Dilation is a myth.

author: @andrewbodor4891
text: Equivalence of Mass Time Dilation AND Speed Time Dilation By Csaba A. Bodor; March 1, 2022 The twin paradox disappears if viewed in this context. In both the things that are in common are (1) the aether, and; (2) gravity. Baryonic matter, including electromagnetic waves, and the aether cannot mix. The aether is pushed aside by the matter BUT pushes back against the matter in the form of, what we call, gravity. The greater the mass, the greater the push. Even with this push there is a large amount of space between the components of the matter. The push, gravity, however, affects those components by pressing on them and slowing down all the properties of matter. Wave length, frequency, spin, speed of movement, everything. Including time. So, the greater the push back of the aether, the greater the time dilation or slower movement of time. Yes, time is a indirect component of baryonic matter. With speed dilation there are similarities and differences. The, as i said, aether resists change. Matter disrupts the aether's symmetry and the aether fights back with a push. The aether also dislikes matter when the matter pushes against it in the form of motion or speed. Moving matter is like something moving through air or water; both mediums resist the motion. The aether pushes back against the push of matter causing the same disruptions it does with baryonic matter. Everything is slowed down including time. Time dilation, again, comes into being. Gravity comes into being, as with when the mass disrupts the aether. Here it is speed that disrupts the aether and creates gravity, not mass. Time dilation, whether caused by mass or speed, is caused by the gravity created by the aether pressing on "stationary" mass or a moving mass. The time dilation is proportional to the amount and-or speed of the mass. Can speed time dilation and its associated gravity be created artificially? If an element or isotope if an element were to be massive enough AND it could be sped up enough, perhaps. How? Manufacturing such element into a disk that could spin at a high enough speed would not be practical; the centripetal forces and vibrations would probably tear the apparatus apart. What if a sufficiently large amount of such element, however, could be forced to vibrate at a very high frequency? The motion of the protons and neutrons moving and vibrating, even though in extremely small sub atomic distances, might get fast enough to affect the aether inside and outside that element to create the gravity needed to cause time dilation. The frequency would need to be very high. Perhaps such a setup could create speed induced artificial gravity. Bob Lazar, if you read this, hope it helps.

author: @AlphaFoxDelta
text: This movie is so important and amazing it is hard to put into words. Firstly, how it accurately presents the concept of time dilation as a very real consequence of the natural laws of this universe. How if you orbit a black hole, or indeed, and severely warped region of spacetime due to the presence of high mass and small volume, or exotic matter *maybe* that you will experience time much more slowly correlated with the amount of warping. You can return the same age to your children who are now older than you or even dead. Secondly, the idea of higher dimensions of space time and the beings that inhabit them is stunningly accurate with our current theories. Just as it is impossibly hard for us to imagine stretching across or enveloping infinite space, it is conversely hard for a higher dimensional being to experience or squeeze into a single point in time and space. We try to stretch infinitely big and cannot, and they try to squeeze into a point infinitesimally small in 4D spacetime and cannot. A higher dimensional being wouldn't be able to exist at just one point, and would need to coax a 4D being, a human, into doing it whatever it is they need to do. This movie is truly *next level*

author: @DoritoWorldOrder
text: The idea that it was hyper-evolved "future-humans" that created the wormhole at Saturn, and Gargantua, and the 5-dimensional library inside it, and saved Cooper from disintegration, makes no sense. It's a bootstrap paradox. If Cooper's actions to transmit the quantum data back to Murph were necessary for the survival of humanity, then humanity would not have survived to evolve towards mastery of the 4th and 5th dimensions and create the wormhole, Gargantua, and the library that allowed Cooper to transmit the data back to Murph. The "future humans" could not be the survivors of Edmunds/Brand's colony on the 3rd and final planet, because Edmunds/Brand would have never been able to discover or travel to that planet without the future humans having created the wormhole connecting our solar system with those systems, and thus there would be no future humans. What would make more sense is that there was an "original" timeline not portrayed in the movie, wherein in the absence of the wormhole connecting our solar system to other regions of space, the group of scientists who prepared the space mission in the movie's timeline would have had no reason to use their last precious few decades and resources to prepare for a space mission because there would have been no wormhole for them to discover as a means of escaping the solar system; instead they would have invested their time and resources trying to perfect transhuman neural networks and/or artificial intelligence, leaving behind intelligent machines and computer networks who could survive on the ruined Earth unaffected by the pollution and lack of food, water, etc—needing only electricity that could be provided by solar energy nuclear fission. text: So, not all scientists think Einstein was correct about this. What we call "time$ is an abstraction of "magnitude of energy or mass required to influence/change". If you think about it this way: it makes sense that more mass/energy is required to influence/change things when inside the event horizon of a black hole: more gravity. But that doesn't mean that things happening outside the event horizon are happening "quicker" it just means they require less energy/mass to influence/change. In that respect there wouldn't be any time delta: we would all exist on the same present (there is no future or past in anything but dreams and history books).

author: @Sincemotivations
text: A gravitational singularity is a fascinating and complex concept in physics, primarily associated with black holes. Here's a breakdown of what it entails: * Definition: * A gravitational singularity, also known as a spacetime singularity, is a point in spacetime where the gravitational field becomes infinitely strong. * This means that the curvature of spacetime becomes infinite, and the laws of physics as we understand them break down. * Key Characteristics: * Infinite Density: At a singularity, matter is thought to be crushed to infinite density. * Breakdown of Spacetime: Spacetime itself ceases to exist in its usual form. * Location: Singularities are believed to exist at the center of black holes. * Theoretical Challenges: * Our current understanding of gravity, based on Einstein's theory of general relativity, predicts the existence of singularities. However, general relativity doesn't provide a complete description of what happens at these points. * A theory of quantum gravity is needed to fully understand the nature of singularities. This is because at this point where gravity is so strong, quantum effects become very important. * Therefore, gravitational singularities represent a point where general relativity and quantum mechanics meet, and where our current understanding of physics is incomplete. * Black Holes: * The most well-known context for gravitational singularities is within black holes. * When a massive star collapses, it can form a black hole, with all its mass concentrated at a central singularity. * The event horizon of a black hole is the boundary beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape the gravitational pull of the singularity. In essence, gravitational singularities are regions of extreme gravity where the fabric of spacetime is disrupted, posing fundamental questions about the nature of the universe.

text: The gravity of Miller's planet doesn't have to be higher at all, in fact even if this planet was the mass of our Moon it would make virtually no difference. The extreme dilation is due to Gargantua, not the planet itself. The planet is in (what seems to be) stable orbit around Gargamtua, so the astronauts on the planet would not feel any additional acceleration from Gargantua itself, but only the planet's effect since they are well within it's gravitational well and are not orbiting, but have landed. The reason the time dilation regime is so much different between the astronaut left behind in the ship (which is NOT orbiting Gargantua) is because he is not in the gravity well of Gargantua, but Miller's planet obviously is. So this means the ship in space with the 1 guy left behind already has exit velocity relative to Gargantua, whereas the 3 people on Miller's planet don't. Tldr: Miller's planet's gravity has virtually no effect on time dilation compared to Gargantua, it could have had 1% of Earth's g for all we care.

author: @gumbilicious1
text: After learning about relativity from more rigorous resources I have started having strong appreciation for how misleading and confusing many of these videos/explanations are. The whole "Time moves slower/faster" flies in the face of relativity. For the person going through these situations time never slows or quickens, their clock keeps trudging along without any noticeable difference. Time passing at different rates will not be noticed until compared to another reference frame, and both of these reference frames will have observers noticing no difference in how fast their personal clock progresses, they'll only notice how clocks in other reference frames move at different rates. Indeed, a huge part of relativity is that all these reference frames are completely valid, stating that 'time passes slower' in a reference frame insinuates there is some True Master Clock keeping The Universe's Time and that your clock is slower than The Clock. This is inaccurate to the model of General Relativity, all clocks are equally valid and beyond that you will never observe your personal clock moving faster or slower, you will only see clocks in other reference frames moving at different rates than your own. I am probably making a bit much of this, but until I grasped this concept my understanding of this subject was limited to regurgitating sound bites from videos I watched without understanding the subject on any deeper or intuitive level

text: 9:20 "There is simply no planet that can have this kind of gravity..." Wait what?....the entire video you were talking about the extreme time dilation being caused because of "Miller's" planet being in PROXIMITY to the event horizon of the black hole. Then you seem to change it and imply it is the planet??? Now I fail to see why the gravity of the planet itself relative to the people on the planet has anything to do with the extreme time dilation. It is an effect of the proximity to the black hole....NOT because they landed on the planet. It is because they are CLOSER to the black hole. If the planet and the people on it are BOTH in the same relativistic reference frame...then it does not matter what gravity the planet has. What matters is the difference between the reference frame of the planet (where it is in proximity to the black hole) and the reference frame of the earth (or the orbiting vehicle waiting for them to come back from the planet. The orbiting vehicle would also have to be orbiting the black hole (at a much farther distance from the event horizon) and NOT just orbiting the planet. As large as those massive waves were in the movie... the planet would actually be more like a white hot ball of plasma spiraling closer and closer to the event horizon. text: Let me start by saying that I quite enjoyed interstellar. ;) I think the premise in the movie is that the planet is orbiting so close to the black hole that it is being affected by the black hole's time dilation - which does in fact become extreme as you approach the event horizon. However, there are still several problems with this. Problem 1: You need to be closer to the black hole. MUCH closer. In order to get time dilation anywhere near this extreme, the surface of the planet would need to be within a few meters of the event horizon, even on a massive black hole like Gargantua. Assuming Miller's Planet has a diameter of just ten thousand km, the difference in the passage of time between the near and far sides of it would be greater than 100 to 1, and the planet would have long ago been shredded to dust by the tidal force not just of gravity, but of TIME ITSELF (techically the people are going to have a similar problem. Time would be passing 10x faster at your head than your feet or vice versa. This is probably really bad for your health. Very extremely bad. To their credit, the writers sort of depict the effect of these extreme tides in the form of the weird super-waves that constantly encircle the planet - but those effects are still far, far smaller than they should be. That planet would be shredded into virtually microscopic bits at that level of time dilation. Problem 2: Going down to the planet doesn't cause time to slow down - going near the black hole does. The ship in orbit would be just as screwed. Even if we handwave away the need to nearly be touching the black hole and the problems with tidal time dilation, the ship is still about as close to the black hole as the planet itself - which means the ship should suffer similar time dilation on the plus side, this means whatsisname isn't an old man. On the negative side, it means they spent a lot more time in a state of extreme time dilation. Fun movie though. I forgive them for most of their handwaving. Except for the power of love thing, that was corny as hell.

author: @Jesse_359
text: You have to get really close to a black hole to experience serious time dilation. If the black hole were the mass of 10 suns, you'd have to get within 10km of the event horizon to experience a 2-1 time dilation (1 second passing for each 2s of a distant observer). The movie suggested a time ratio of about 1-61360 (3hrs = 21yrs), which would put you at most millimeters above the event horizon to achieve. Even for a massive 1 billion solar mass black hole, the planet would essentially have to be sitting ON the event horizon to achieve those values. The best you could realistically hope for might be 1/10 ratio, with a planet sitting around 0.2 AU away from the event horizon of a galactic scale black hole, but I think any such orbit would be wildly unstable. Also the ship orbiting the planet would experience almost exactly the same time dilation. It would have to move fairly far away for the difference to become significant.

If the black hole were the mass of 10 suns, you would have to get within 10km of the event horizon to experience a 2-1 time dilation (1 second passing for each 2s of a distant observer). The movie suggested a time ratio of about 1-61360 (3hrs = 21yrs), which would put you at most millimeters above the event horizon to achieve. Even for a massive 1 billion solar mass black hole, the planet would essentially have to be sitting ON the event horizon to achieve those values. The best you could realistically hope for might be 1/10 ratio, with a planet sitting around 0.2 AU away from the event horizon of a galactic scale black hole, but I think any such orbit would be wildly unstable. author: @nulzmusic8461
text: So, we see that Cooper ended up inside the tesseract, a 5 dimensional space designed by "they". What we need to understand is that the 5th dimension allows us to see the parallel universes or the alternate realities. So, to us what seemed like Cooper looking at his own past from inside the tesseract was actually him looking at an alternate reality of himself and Murph. That is the big secret of Interstellar. And if you look it from that perspective everything seems fall into place and all the questions seems to have been answered. ******** Who were "They"? *********** The human species gets suffocated due to blight and become extinct. The only survivors were some scientists and engineers, probably at NASA who survived cause they stayed underground. They carried on with their research underground and lived that way and carried human species forward for years to come, and may be after a few decades or after 100 years or so, they were able to access the higher dimensions, by using a tesseract and placing it near the singularity of some super massive blackhole, cause at singularity the time stops and hence, they could have access to infinite space and time, and that allowed them to access the higher dimensions, the 4th and the 5th dimensions. So, these survivors were "They", the so called beings of the 5th dimension. "They" found a new home for human beings of the past, the Edmund's planet in a distant galaxy, and placed a worm hole near Saturn to help them reach there. Now, they needed a person from the past, smart enough to whom they could give the quantum data using gravity, who could solve the equation of gravity. They must have shortlisted a few such people (Murph being one of them), but there was a PROBLEM.. ******* THE PROBLEM ********* Sending the quantum data using gravitational anomaly to chosen these people would have worked only if 1. that person was a physicist working on the equation of gravity. ****************** CONDITION 1 2. the data would come from someone with whom this person shared a strong bond of Love. ******************* CONDITION 2 Only once these 2 conditions are met, that data would make any sense to that chosen person. So, 1. they needed to get this person to NASA so that he/she would be aligned with task of resolving the equation of gravity.************ to tackle CONDITION 1 2. they needed to get someone, with whom this person shared a strong bond of love, inside the tesseract near a singularity, so that this person would use gravity to send the quantum data from inside the tesseract, to the chosen one on earth hoping that the bond of love they share, will do the trick. ************ to tackle CONDITION 2 So, out of those chosen ones, they chose Murph cause she shared that strong bond of love with her father who also happened to be an Astronaut with NASA, and he could be somehow lead to the tesseract in the outer space, and they felt that they could use this father-daughter duo of Joseph and Murphy Cooper to make this mission a success. We were shown that after the crash Cooper left NASA and became a farmer and later he got the news that NASA has been shut down. Later when NASA was Re-instated as a Secret organization, cooper was not aware of NASA being still operational. He receives NASA coordinates through a gravitational anomaly and He and Murph reach NASA n there he finds out that NASA is actually still operational. Cooper goes on the Lazarus Mission through the wormhole and jumps into the event horizon of Gargantua. ******* THE PARALLEL UNIVERSE ******* Remember Murphy's law, everything that can happen will happen. So, when we were shown that after the crash Cooper left NASA and became a farmer, in some parallel universe he continued to be an Astronaut with NASA even after NASA became a secret organization. And cause they had access to infinite space and time and the 5th dimension, "they" could observe that parallel universe too. So, it turns out that “they" could observe both the versions of Cooper in 2 parallel universes. 1. Cooper(the farmer) 2. Cooper(the Astronaut) In that other universe too, they placed a wormhole near Saturn and Cooper(the Astronaut) captained endurance through that wormhole, and as per Murphy's law, in that universe too if he would have a choice of jumping inside Gargantua's event horizon, he would. ******* THE BIG HIDDEN SECRET ABOUT LAZARUS MISSION ********* Christopher Nolan gave mission the name "Lazarus Mission", which implies someone had to die and then come back from the dead. The big secret here is that the Cooper (the Farmer) that we see jumping inside the tesseract in the movie dies as soon as he jumps inside the event horizon. And the Cooper that we see later inside the tesseract is the Cooper(the Astronaut) from the parallel universe, and he is the one who is dragged into the parallel universe of Cooper (farmer) inside the tesseract by "They" and he is the one who later reaches the Cooper Station. So, Cooper (the farmer) dies and comes back from the dead, from a parallel universe as Cooper (the Astronaut). that is why Christopher Nolan chose the name "Lazarus Mission" for this mission. ******* THE SWITCH ********* The switch from Cooper (the farmer) to Cooper (the Astronaut) was made when Cooper (the farmer) jumps into the Event Horizon of Gargantua. There was an untimely and relatively unnecessary Cut sequence there, where the scene switches back to earth, for apparently no reason. Here's how it went. In that scene we see: 1. Cooper(the farmer)'s space craft catching fire soon after he detaches from endurance. (Location: inside Gargantua) 2. Cooper(the farmer) in pain (Location: inside Gargantua) ------ CUT SEQUENCE ------- 3. Cooper(the farmer)'s corn field on fire (Location: Earth) 4. Cooper(the farmer)'s son watching helplessly in despair. (Location: Earth) 5. Murph filled with hopelessness, looking at the broken replica of the moon lander that her father gave to her. (Location: Earth) So, here everything that belongs to or is related to Cooper(the farmer) is shown as kinda broken/on fire, indicating that Cooper (the farmer)'s world is coming to an end and this is where we say good bye to Cooper(the farmer). ******* INSIDE THE TESSERACT ********* Right after that cut sequence the movie makes a switch from Cooper(the farmer) to Cooper(the Astronaut) who jumped inside Gargantua may be decades ago. So, when Cooper(the Astronaut) who jumped inside Gargantua in that parallel universe, at that time, Cooper(the farmer) was probably living on that farm with Murph. The Cooper that we see inside the Tesseract is the Cooper(the Astronaut) from the parallel universe who has been dragged into the universe of Cooper(the farmer) inside the tesseract by "they". Here, upon seeing Murph from inside the tesseract he realizes that he is looking at a Murph from a parallel universe and initially he feels that he has failed in his mission, so he feels that in that universe of Cooper(the farmer), he should make them STAY together, hence he sends the STAY message. Then after TARS (not the TARS we saw earlier, this is TARS from the parallel universe of Cooper(the Astronaut)) tells him about the tesseract, Cooper(the Astronaut) eventually realizes that "they didn't choose him, they chose Murph to save the world". Now everything becomes clear to him, and he, 1. gives out the NASA's coordinates to Murph and Cooper(the Farmer), so that Cooper would take Murph to NASA ********* TO FULFIL THE CONDITION 1 ********** 2. gives the quantum data through the watch. ********* TO FULFIL THE CONDITION 2 ********** Once, both the conditions are met, "they" know that his job there was done and hence, they close the tesseract and send Cooper(the Astronaut) back through the wormhole after which he is rescued and taken back to the Cooper station. Now as "they" have access to infinite space and time, "they" make Cooper(the Astronaut) travel through the wormhole at the time when endurance, with Cooper(the farmer) inside was going through the wormhole in the opposite direction. There Cooper(the Astronaut) distorts spacetime to create an impression of a handshake with Brand. **** WHY COOPER(THE FARMER) **** So, when Cooper(the Astronaut) jumped into Gargantua, "they" dragged him into Cooper(the farmer)'s parallel universe, Why did they do it that way? Why did they not let him be in his own universe, of Cooper(the Astronaut)? The answer is cause that would never have worked out. If from inside the tesseract, Cooper(The Astronaut) would give out the NASA's coordinates back himself (Cooper(The Astronaut)) of the past. Then Cooper(The Astronaut) of the past would have known where those coordinates lead to, cause he worked with NASA (the secret organization), and that being a top government secret, he would have never shared that information with Murph and hence, CONDITION 1 would not have met. So, they had to create a parallel universe for Cooper in which he would think that NASA has been shut down and would not be aware of the fact that NASA was later re-instated. To make that happen, they create a Gravitational anomaly to crash Cooper's spacecraft (the one he had a nightmare about in the beginning of the movie) to somehow force him to quit NASA and hence, created a parallel universe of Cooper(the farmer). When Cooper(the farmer) received the NASA's coordinates, he had no idea what those coordinates lead to and accidentally ended up taking Murph to NASA, hence fulfilling the CONDITION 1. That for me is the Plot of Interstellar. There was no time loop or bootstrap paradox. In the 5th dimension there never is.

Then after TARS (not the TARS we saw earlier, this is TARS from the parallel universe of Cooper(the Astronaut)) tells him about the tesseract, Cooper(the Astronaut) eventually realizes that "they did not choose him, they chose Murph to save the world". Now everything becomes clear to him, and he, 1. gives out the NASA's coordinates to Murph and Cooper(the Farmer), so that Cooper would take Murph to NASA ********* TO FULFIL THE CONDITION 1 ********** 2. gives the quantum data through the watch. ********* TO FULFIL THE CONDITION 2 ********** Once, both the conditions are met, "they" know that his job there was done and hence, they close the tesseract and send Cooper(the Astronaut) back through the wormhole after which he is rescued and taken back to the Cooper station. Now as "they" have access to infinite space and time, "they" make Cooper(the Astronaut) travel through the wormhole at the time when endurance, with Cooper(the farmer) inside was going through the wormhole in the opposite direction. There Cooper(the Astronaut) distorts spacetime to create an impression of a handshake with Brand. **** WHY COOPER(THE FARMER) **** So, when Cooper(the Astronaut) jumped into Gargantua, "they" dragged him into Cooper(the farmer)'s parallel universe, Why did they do it that way? When Cooper(the farmer) received the NASA's coordinates, he had no idea what those coordinates lead to and accidentally ended up taking Murph to NASA, hence fulfilling the CONDITION 1. author: @akkalat85
text: Everyone keeps suggesting there is a paradox concerning the 5D future humans and their ability to save humanity in the past. It's really not a paradox at all. Everyone assumes humanity survived to ascend to the 5th dimension but how could humanity exist in the future if not for the actions of Cooper.. who was guided by future humans (begin endless loop). Amelia Brand carried on with the rest of her mission (thanks to Cooper). I postulate that Brand used the human seeds as intended and set up a colony. A colony that would thrive and eventually evolve beyond human. Thus Earth is of little importance, and may have indeed died. These colonists, and the generations that followed, would have been told the story of a great man (Cooper) who saved them from extinction. With the ability to manipulate space-time, they would pay homage to their hero "God" by helping him in the past so he may fulfill the mission most important to him, to once again see his daughter. Plan B worked beautifully. But the 5D humans, having the power to bend space-time, decided there's no reason why Plan A had to fail. Or... Earth was never doomed to die. In this scenario Cooper and co. still venture through time and space... except that it didn't matter in the long run. Earth would survive through sheer luck and poor predictions of the magnitude of the blight. But only with enough nourishment to keep a small pocket of humanity from becoming extinct. It is the closest to extinction we have ever been and even countless generations later the impact of this event would no doubt place deep, emotional scars on the descendants. Our technology (for a time) would equate to that of the stone age. It would send human evolution back 500-1000 year. Untold years later the survivors evolve to the 5th dimension and attempt to circumvent the extinction level event and it's impact on the future of humanity. So, humanity survived... but it could have survived better! Or... The entire thing is a simulation. A simulated universe, with simulated constants and variables. It could be that the 5D humans are programmers. They live in the bulk universe, while we live in their elaborate simulated universe. The events depicted on film is the result of a block of code containing an (unintentional) infinite loop. Brace yourself, this might get a little geeky: Imagine they instantiate a human object named Cooper in a function/method used to populate the simulated Earth. During one iteration while the programmers were testing different techniques to correct the code, accidentally sent the Cooper object outside the scope of the local function/method and into the main body of the program represented by the tesseract. He now sees the true scope of the program and has access to areas normally restricted, but only in a limited sense because he isn't supposed to be there. Think of the singularity in a black hole as a kind of return statement that sends object values to the beginning of it's main story (main body of code). The Cooper object has it's values returned the main body (beginning of film), but the actual object still remains trapped in the block, only it's value was passed. What would that look like if we represented it in 4 dimensions? Probably something like a ghost, because it wouldn't really be Cooper, it would just be his return value. Leonard Susskind hypothesized that objects passing through a black hole, in a sense, split at the firewall. The outside observer thinks the object was simply erased from the universe because no information can be exchanged due to the speed of light, but the information pertaining to that object still exists. This duality is manifesting in 2 distinctly different Coopers, one that is physical, and one that only exists as information. Cooper is doomed to remain locked in the erroneous code block until the higher level programmer solves his own algorithmic problem (represented by the gravity equation). You have to imagine this loop running through many iterations before the code would be configured in such a way as to send the Cooper object outside the localities of the method in which it's created. The 5D beings manipulate the code, testing all possibilities, just like Murph's name. Heck, there could even be 6D beings programming the 5D beings, programming the 4D beings (us), programming the 3D beings (working 3D models with applied textures), programming the 2D beings (cartoons, drawings, animation). As you can see, at each level the working objects believe themselves to be real with no way to access knowledge of the the greater workings a level above. But just as we can manipulate 2D or 3D objects, a 5th dimensional being would have the ability to manipulate all dimensions beneath it. We enjoy manipulating lower dimensions for no other reason than "because we can". Q. So why did they help us? A. That might have just been a side effect of higher level code manipulation. Perhaps this is the iteration where the programmers test out what would happen if Earth was given a fighting chance. Q. Why would they do this? A. Why not? Curiosity and experimentation are the very core of computer programming! Q. It can't be! A. Someone once said: If you accept the fact that we humans can run some pretty complex simulations, and you accept the fact that new universes are born every time we play games like Skyrim or GTA, and you accept the fact that at any given time there exist more active "avatars" than humans... suddenly the chances that you really exist becomes very small. It's more probable that we are avatars created by beings a dimension above ours. That's a troubling thought. Q. What if you're wrong... about everything? A. I probably am!

Thats why Cooper was able to escape the tesseract. It collapsed because Cooper saved humanity through Plan A, and therefore the tesseract no longer existed. The entire paradox within the movie was closed because the future humans sacrificed themselves to save humanity. Plan A was successful, and humanity lives happily ever after on Brand's planet.

text: Good breakdown. What always gets me about this movie is that Murphy’s law is all the way through it. If they hadn’t gone to Miller’s planet first and lost time, Murph would still be a child back on earth when they got back to Endurance. If Mann hadn’t faked his data bringing them to him and then partially destroyed the Endurance causing them to get away from Mann’s planet, they wouldn’t have been caught by Gargantua for Cooper to do his thing and Brand to get to Edmund’s planet. At the end after all those years, Cooper wouldn’t have lived if all that time hadn’t passed where humanity was on the station near Saturn, catching him before his O2 ran out. So Miller, Mann, years lost were all meant to happen for humanity to survive. Since a future humanity created the wormhole meant everything in the movie had to happen how it did, or there would be no wormhole. It’s likely the older Brand already knew this too, so I don’t think of his character badly. He knew they’d succeed, so built the station. Fun stuff you’ll notice in the movie: there are no birds on Earth. You don’t see them or hear any. Oops.

author: @ErwinSchrodinger64
text: Movie made perfect sense. However, it was important to understand the basics of quantum gravity. The point of traveling to the other solar system wasn't the new planets. It was to travel inside the super massive black hole, Gargantua, to understand the equations of quantum gravity so we could learn how to "control" gravity. The only black holes we can approach are super massive black holes (stellar mass black holes would "spaghettify" anything venturing too close to it). Thus, by controlling gravity we could build spaceships by manipulating gravity itself and not relying on rockets which would be too costly and impossible to travel to the stars. Kip Thorne, the producer and scientific advisor wrote a book called The Science of Interstellar. Amongst the scientific community, Dr. Thorne is an expert in black hole physics via Einstein's field equations. Nolan and Thorne worked exhaustively on making the physics correct for the film. Nolan, at times, was very frustrated when Dr. Thorne explained to Nolan certain scenes wouldn't work because they would be physically impossible. In effect, Dr. Thorne would have to exhaustively work out solutions, mathematically, to make the physics "work" on what Nolan was attempting to achieve. What's more amazing is Nolan spent an incredible amount of money on the relativistic physics of black holes that several research papers were written on the matter. Christopher Nolan is incredible director, in the sense, he hired one of the greatest minds in science and told Thorne, if it's not physical possible we can not put it in this film. Dr. Thorne even showed Nolan on how bizarre the spatial and time parameters are around black holes and Nolan said while visually fascinating, there is no way the majority of audiences could even comprehend what they were looking at. The mathematics that you see on the board, throughout the film, specifically, is applied differential geometry on manifolds, coupled with Lagrangian and Hamiltonian dynamics. Personally, differential geometry is incredibly difficult mathematics and makes up the majority of Einstein's field equations. It's also utilized in quantum mechanics.

text: My favourite film of all time. So sad that many didn't get it and couldn't appreciate it for a masterpiece that it is. This film changed me... It taught me about time and space being relative. Possibility of being able to view time as a space dimension, i.e. being able to "see" all the moments of time at once. Warping of space. Gravity.. Other dimensions... Making decisions for the greater good vs for the selfish reasons...etc etc Man, Interstellar explored so many interesting themes. And the visuals on it were absolutely amazing - so glad that I saw it on the big screen first. Also, Hans Zimmer's score is breathtaking - one of the best of all time. The film is magic, except that it's not. It's science. It's real. It's true. And so many people don't get it, so they don't like it. Or just focus on the "love" message and write the film of as too chic flick. I pitty them. This film can change your whole worldview if you go see it with an open mind and without being afraid to not understand some parts of it. And you must watch it on the biggest screen you can find!!
